items.stem: Describe any three main features of ‘Alluvial soil’ found in India.
items.answer: Alluvial soil is counted among the most fertile of all Indian soil types. It is made up of sand, silt and clay laid down chiefly as silt by the Indus–Ganga–Brahmaputra river system. It also carries an ample amount of potash, phosphoric acid and lime, which is why it supports intensive cultivation over the northern plains.

items.stem: Describe any three main features of ‘Black soil’ found in India.
items.answer: Black soil is fine textured and clayey in nature and is particularly suited to growing cotton. It holds a high proportion of lime, iron and magnesium but generally low quantities of phosphorus, nitrogen and organic matter. It is formed from weathered lava rock, which gives it its black colour, and its high clay content makes it highly retentive of moisture and extremely fertile in most places where it occurs.

items.stem: Describe the different steps of ‘resource planning.’
items.answer: Resource planning is a complex process carried out in three steps. First, resources are identified and inventoried region by region, which involves surveying, mapping and both qualitative and quantitative estimation and measurement of the resources. Second, a planning structure is evolved with the appropriate technology, skill and institutional set-up needed to implement resource development plans. Third, the resource development plans are matched with the overall national development plans.

items.stem: Suggest any three ways to improve health and nutritional status of people in India.
items.answer: Health and nutrition can be improved by eating healthy food every day so that the body stays fit; by checking that fruit is clean before eating it, since unclean fruit causes disease; and by taking Vitamin C rich fruit such as grapes, apples and oranges daily.

items.stem: Classify resources on the basis of origin.
items.answer: On the basis of origin resources are of two kinds. Biotic resources are all the living organisms of our environment — trees, animals, insects and the like. Abiotic resources are all the non-living things present in the environment, such as earth, air, water, metals and rocks.

items.stem: State any two goals of development other than income.
items.answer: Income is only one aspect of life; two other goals of development are equal treatment, security and dignity for all citizens, and a safe and secure environment in which women can make progress in every walk of their life.

items.stem: How can two persons have different developmental goals?
items.answer: Different persons hold different notions of development because their life situations differ. What is development for one may not be development for another and may even be destructive for him. For example, an industrialist may want more dams for electricity, but the same dams submerge land and disrupt the lives of the people who are displaced.

items.stem:
What are resources ? State the important characteristics of resources.
or
What are resource ? Describe their two feature.
items.answer: All the useful elements of the environment that satisfy human needs are called resources. Their chief characteristics are that they are free gifts of nature and useful elements of the environment, that they are technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable, that they satisfy the basic needs of man, and that they are limited in quantity.

items.stem: What are renewable resources ? Which processes are used to renew them ?
items.answer: Renewable resources are those that can be used again because they are reproduced or replenished, such as crops and trees. They are renewed through physical, chemical and mechanical processes. They are also called continuous flow resources; solar energy, wind energy, water power, forests and wildlife are examples.

items.stem: What can be the harmful result of indiscriminate use of resources ?
items.answer: Indiscriminate use of resources amounts to self-destruction. To meet the greed of a few individuals resources get depleted at a rapid speed. The accumulation of resources in a few hands divides society into the haves and the have-nots, which is unjust and dangerous for harmonious development. It also leads to global crises such as depletion of the ozone layer, pollution of the environment, land degradation and global warming.

items.stem: Distinguish between human made resources and natural resources. Give two distinctions.
items.answer: Natural resources are gifts of nature, whereas human made resources are created by man. Natural resources are of two types, biotic (plants and animals) and abiotic (rocks and metals), while human made resources are developed by man using his skill and knowledge by utilising natural resources, for example machines and technology.

items.stem: Mention any three measures of conservation of resources.
items.answer: Resources can be conserved by using them judiciously and carefully, by preventing their wastage and misuse, and by using alternatives or substitutes in the case of non-renewable resources.
items.ocr: The answer runs from page 14 into the top of page 15.

items.stem: ‘Resources are a function of human activities’. Explain.
items.answer: The natural endowments of the environment are nature's free gift, but they become resources only when man puts them to use. In that sense resources are a function of human activity: human beings transform the material available in the environment into resources, as a carpenter transforms wood into furniture. Human beings are therefore an essential component of every resource.

items.stem: How is climate the most important factor in soil formation ? Explain two reasons.
items.answer: Climate is the leading agent in soil formation because it decides the rate of weathering and the type of vegetation that grows. Rocks exposed to sunlight expand during the day and contract in the evening when the sun goes down, and this repeated expansion and contraction cracks them. When rain falls at night the water enters those cracks, and as the temperature drops the water freezes and widens the cracks further, so the rock is easily broken down and eroded by running water.

items.stem: Explain the major factors which are responsible for the formation of soil.
items.answer: Relief, parent rock or bed rock, climate, vegetation, other forms of life and time are the important factors in the formation of soil. Forces of nature such as change in temperature, the action of running water, wind and glaciers and the activity of decomposers all contribute to it. Chemical and organic changes taking place within the soil are equally important, and the finished soil consists of both organic (humus) and inorganic material.

items.stem:
What steps can be taken to promote soil conservation?
or
Suggest any three measures of soil conservation.
items.answer: Ploughing along the contour lines stops water running down the slopes; this is contour ploughing. On steep slopes steps can be cut to make terraces, and terrace cultivation restricts erosion. Large fields can be divided into strips with strips of grass left to grow between the crops, which breaks the force of the wind; this is strip cropping. Rows of trees planted to create shelter, called shelter belts, work in the same way.

items.stem: What do you know about Earth Summit ? What were its aims ?
items.answer: In June 1992 more than 100 heads of state met at Rio de Janeiro in Brazil for the first International Earth Summit. It was convened to address the urgent problems of environmental protection and socio-economic development at the global level. The assembled leaders signed the declaration on Global Climate Change and on Biological Diversity, and the Rio Convention endorsed the Global Forest Principles and adopted Agenda 21 for achieving sustainable development in the 21st century.

items.stem: Distinguish between stock and reserve giving one example of each.
items.answer: Stocks are those materials which have the potential to satisfy human needs but cannot be utilised because we lack the technical know-how; minerals found in the sea bed or under the oceans are an example. Reserves are that part of the stock for which we do have the technical know-how but which is not in use at present; forests and reservoirs are examples.

items.stem: Distinguish between natural resources and cultural resources.
items.answer: Resources provided to us by nature are called natural resources; land, water, minerals and forests are of this kind. Resources created by human beings are called cultural resources; science and technology, engineering, machines, buildings, monuments and paintings, as well as social institutions such as associations and families, are all cultural resources.

items.stem:
‘Land is a prime resource’. Explain the statement.
or
What are the main advantages of India’s land under a variety of relief features ?
items.answer: Land is a prime resource because all types of organisms, man included, are born, flourish, mature and finally meet their end on land. Land provides every necessity of life — food, clothing and shelter — and without land no organism could survive, nor could its existence even be imagined. Land, given to us by nature, is therefore the prime resource.

items.stem: Since the land under pasture has reduced, what impact it had on cattle-rearing ? Explain two points.
items.answer: Only about 4% of India's land is under permanent pasture, and this shortage has told badly on cattle rearing. Because pastures are lacking, there is tremendous pressure of the livestock population on agricultural land, and cattle have to be reared on farm waste, grain chaff and a few fodder crops instead of on grazing land.

items.stem: What do you know about Agenda-21 ? What were its aims ?
items.answer: Agenda-21 is the declaration signed by world leaders in 1992 at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held at Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It aims at achieving global sustainable development, combating environmental damage, poverty and disease through global co-operation based on common interests, mutual needs and shared responsibilities. One of its major objectives is that every local government should draw up its own local Agenda-21.

items.stem: In which parts of India laterite soils are found? State the crops supported by this soil.
items.answer: Laterite soils occur mainly in Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh and the hilly regions of Orissa and Assam. In the hilly areas of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu the soil suits the growth of tea and coffee, while the red laterite soils of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala are more suitable for crops such as cashew nuts.

items.stem: “All biotic resources are not renewable”. Discuss the statement.
items.answer: The biosphere is the source of all biotic resources, which include forests, agricultural crops and wildlife; coal and petroleum are also biotic because they originated from organic matter buried in the earth's interior millions of years ago. Forests, fish and crops are renewable, but coal and petroleum are not: they are exhaustible on a large scale and take an extremely long time to be renewed. Hence not all biotic resources are renewable.

items.stem:
What do you understand by conservation of resources for sustainable benefit of the present as well as future generations ?
or
Define the concept conservation of resources. Why is it necessary ?
items.answer: Conservation is the judicious and planned use of natural resources for the sustainable benefit of the present generation while maintaining the potential to meet the needs and aspirations of future generations. It is necessary because our resources are limited in nature and must be used judiciously, because many of them are non-renewable and need extra care, and because conserving them is essential for our own sustenance and for the ongoing process of economic development.

items.answer: Resource planning involves three steps. Finally these resource development plans are matched with the overall national development plans.

items.stem:
What is soil erosion ? Mention two main causes of it.
or
What is soil erosion ? Write two human activities that lead to soil erosion.
items.answer: Soil erosion is the removal of top soil on a large scale from one place to another by natural agents such as wind, water and air, or by human activity. Running water cuts through clayey soil and carves deep channels called gullies, leaving the soil unfit for cultivation. Deforestation increases the frequency of floods, which damage soils extensively. In dry and sandy areas wind is the main agent, blowing away exposed loose top soil and depositing it elsewhere. Reckless felling of trees and overgrazing destroy the vegetation cover that would otherwise protect the soil.

items.stem: Explain three types of soil erosion.
items.answer: Gully erosion occurs where running water cuts through clayey soils and makes deep channels called gullies; the land becomes unfit for cultivation and is known as badland. Sheet erosion occurs when water flows as a sheet over large areas down a slope and the top layer of soil is washed away. Wind erosion occurs when wind blows off loose, dry soil from flat and sloping land.

items.stem: Give the distribution of alluvial soils in brief.
items.answer: The entire northern plain is made of alluvial soil. It has been deposited by the three great Himalayan river systems — the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra. These soils also extend into Rajasthan and Gujarat through a narrow corridor, and they are found again in the eastern coastal plains, in the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri rivers.

items.stem: The pattern of the net sown area varies greatly from one state to another. It is over 80 per cent of the total area in Punjab and Haryana and less than 10 percent in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and Andaman Nicobar Islands. Find out reasons for the low proportion of net sown area in these states.
items.answer: The net sown area is low in these states because they are inhabited mostly by tribal groups who still practise shifting cultivation, because the states are covered by dense tropical forest, because they receive very heavy rainfall, because their terrain is rocky, and because fertile alluvial soil is lacking there.
